video.title: The Phone Habit That Was Ruining My Life

summary: Nick Huber and a guest (Corey) discuss breaking a phone addiction. Nick turned his phone off from 7pm to 7am, cut screen time to about 2.5 hours a day, batches texts and email into a 4:30-5pm calendar slot, and uses a notepad instead of his phone. The video contains no business idea; the takeaway is that managing attention and being hard to reach improves sleep, relationships and focus for a founder running several companies.

speakers.name: Nick Huber
speakers.description: Sweaty Startup host, runs several companies

speakers.name: Corey
speakers.description: Conversation partner; Nick mentions playing golf with him

tactics.name: Phone off 7pm to 7am
steps: Turn the phone off at 7pm and back on at 7am
If a full phone fast is too hard, start with a shorter window such as 7 to 7 or 8 to 8
Expect discomfort and anxiety at first

quote.text: I'm going to turn my phone off at seven p.m. I'm going to turn it back on at seven a.m.
quote.speaker: Nick Huber

tactics.name: Batch messages into one daily slot
steps: Block 4:30 to 5pm on the calendar to clear all inboxes and texts
Don't reply outside that window; let people wait until the next day
Accept that people close to you will understand

quote.text: I have on my calendar from 4 30 to 5 to clear all my inboxes.
quote.speaker: Nick Huber

tactics.name: Notepad and pencil instead of phone
steps: Carry a notepad and pencil at all times
Write down anything that makes you want to reach for the phone, such as Amazon orders or messages to send
Copy the notes into the phone later, e.g. after a walk

quote.text: keep a note pad and a pencil with you at all times.
quote.speaker: Nick Huber

tactics.name: Swap phones with spouse
steps: Trade phones with your partner so you can't run your usual check routine
Move app-only tasks such as ordering food or the daycare swipe to a shared arrangement first

quote.text: Me and my wife can trade phones now.
quote.speaker: Nick Huber

tactics.name: Phone-free morning walk
steps: Walk about 30 minutes each morning without the phone
Use the time to think about long-term goals
Write down ideas on a notepad

tools_mentioned.name: Slack
tools_mentioned.purpose: Team channel that posts every lead and closed deal to motivate the team; also a distraction source

tools_mentioned.name: Chipotle app
tools_mentioned.purpose: Food ordering, cited as a reason he needed his phone

tools_mentioned.name: Amazon
tools_mentioned.purpose: Shopping, cited as a reason to reach for the phone

tools_mentioned.name: Twitter
tools_mentioned.purpose: Social media cited as a dopamine source

warnings.warning: Constant notifications on leads, closed deals and revenue, plus social media, create a dopamine loop that makes it very hard to stay off the phone.

quote.text: you get notifications every time you close a deal, you get revenue.
quote.speaker: Nick Huber

warnings.warning: Even carrying the phone on a thinking walk leads to checking Slack, email and messages.
Real-time deal and lead feeds are motivating for a team but a slippery slope for the founder.

lessons.lesson: Being slow to respond is acceptable; you don't have to reply to every message or say yes to every request.

quote.text: you don't have to respond. You don't have to jump to do this. You don't have to say yes to every request.
quote.speaker: Nick Huber

lessons.lesson: Batching communications into a fixed daily window protects focus time for a founder running several companies.
Text messaging has become the new email and needs the same triage discipline.

quote.text: Text messaging is the new email.
quote.speaker: Nick Huber

lessons.lesson: Sharing a live Slack feed of leads and closed deals is highly motivating for a team, but the founder may not want to receive it personally.
Leading by example matters for parenting; reducing phone use improved Nick's sleep, relationships and engagement with his kids.
Best ideas and long-term thinking come from unplugged time, so protect it with offline note-taking.

evidence_quality.rationale: Personal anecdote about phone habits with no business idea or verifiable metrics; the only figures are self-reported screen time. The transcript is Whisper tiny with some mis-heard words.
